title: The winds that scatter
hook: by the winds that scatter, and the clouds that carry (51:1–2)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Block C closed, and your line was the middle holds the whole. Which verse came back to you, and who did you tell? Day five hundred ninety-three, and a new block begins.

Block D: towards the thirtieth part. Over the next ten weeks we'll walk from Surah Adh-Dhariyat, the fifty-first, toward the short surahs that close the book. The surahs get shorter from here, and the sound changes. Lines get quicker. Oaths pile up, one after another. And the very first thing this block does is swear by something you can't see, only feel on your face: the wind, the thing that scatters.

Surah Adh-Dhariyat opens with four oaths, each a short line in Arabic. Pickthall's translation of the first two: "By those that winnow with a winnowing, And those that bear the burden (of the rain)." Winnowing is an old farm picture: tossing grain in the air so the wind blows the chaff away. Adh-dhariyat are the scatterers, the winds that lift dust and seed and carry them off. Then al-hamilat, the carriers, bearing a heavy load: the clouds, full of rain. Then al-jariyat, those that run easily, and al-muqassimat, those that distribute by command. The verse doesn't say who these are. It gives only what they do. So people asked. A report preserved by the commentators says 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, preaching in Kufa, invited questions, and someone asked him about these opening words. He answered: the scatterers are the winds, the carriers are the clouds, the runners are the ships, and the distributors are the angels. Wind, cloud, ship and angel. Notice the movement. Wind lifts water to the sky. Cloud carries it. Ships run on the water the wind pushes. And angels distribute, by command, the provision all of it brings. Read that way, ordinary weather becomes a chain of delivery. Why open with an oath? In the Qur'an an oath draws attention: look at this, then hear what follows. The next verses answer the oaths: what you are promised is true, and the judgment will come. The surah swears by ordinary things in motion to make a claim about something no one can yet see.
screen: `FOUR OATHS, FOUR MOVING THINGS.` · `WINNOWING: WIND THAT LIFTS AND SCATTERS.` · `'ALI: WINDS, CLOUDS, SHIPS, ANGELS.` · `WEATHER AS A CHAIN OF DELIVERY.`

segments.voice: The practice: feel the wind today. If you can, step outside or open a window. If not, sit and remember the last wind you felt. Notice where it touches: your face, your hands, the back of your neck. You can't see it. You only know it by what it moves. Watch for something it moves now: a leaf, a curtain, your hair. If you pray, you can say subhanallah, glory to Allah, with each gust. The bell holds the time.
Adh-dhariyat: the winnowing winds of 51:1, which 'Ali read as the first link in a chain of winds, clouds, ships and angels. Today's word.
Your line: by the scattering winds. Today, when the wind moves something near you, stop for one breath and notice what it's carrying. Day five hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: When strong wind blows, Muslims have a supplication taught in hadith that asks for its good and seeks refuge from its harm.

fork.setup: someone in Kufa asks 'Ali what 'those that winnow' are. what does he say?
fork.reveal: winds, then clouds, ships and angels: a chain of delivery from sky to provision.

original.note: Arabic: the scatterers, the winnowing winds; the word that names surah 51.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poetic oath by the weather.
what it means: four oaths by things that move, read as winds, clouds, ships and angels, opening a claim about judgment.
what a scholar hears: the reading comes from a report of 'Ali answering questions in Kufa, preserved by Ibn Kathir and others; the oaths are answered in 51:5–6.
